title: Bánh Flan
subtitle: vietnamese caramel custard
excerpt: Bánh flan is the Vietnamese version of crème caramel, often made with coconut milk and sometimes a splash of coffee for depth. The custard is silky, wobbly, and served with a dark caramel sauce. This recipe makes 6 individual flans.
sourceNotes: Bánh flan is a direct adaptation of the French crème caramel introduced during the colonial period. Vietnamese cooks made it their own by using condensed milk and sometimes adding coffee or coconut milk to the custard.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and keep refrigerated for up to 3 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the flans a day ahead for best results. The custard sets more firmly overnight.
recipe.temperatureNote: Bake in a water bath at 160°C

glossaryTerms.definition: The Vietnamese custard for bánh flan uses condensed milk rather than cream and regular milk. This gives it a denser, sweeter texture than the French original.
A water bath used in baking delicate custards. The moulds sit in a pan of hot water in the oven, which keeps the temperature gentle and prevents the custard from curdling or cracking.

content.text: Bánh flan is a silky Vietnamese custard with a dark caramel base.
The
custard
is made with eggs and condensed milk and baked in a
bain-marie
This recipe makes 6 individual flans.
Do not rush the chilling time. The flans need at least 4 hours in the fridge to set fully before unmoulding.
What you need

items.prepNote: dissolved in 2 tbsp hot water, optional

content.text: Method
Preheat the oven to 160°C. Arrange 6 ramekins or small moulds in a deep baking tin.

Make the caramel: heat the sugar and water in a small pan over medium heat. Do not stir. Cook until it turns a deep amber. Quickly pour a thin layer into the base of each ramekin. Swirl to coat. Leave to set.
Whisk the eggs and egg yolks together lightly in a large bowl. Do not create too many bubbles.
Gently heat the coconut milk and condensed milk together until just warm. Do not boil.
Slowly pour the warm milk mixture into the egg mixture, whisking gently. Add the dissolved coffee if using. Strain through a fine sieve.
Pour the custard into the caramel-lined ramekins. Fill the baking tin with hot water to come halfway up the sides of the ramekins.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the custard is just set with a slight wobble in the centre. Remove from the water bath and cool. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours.
To unmould, run a knife around the edge, place a plate on top, and flip quickly. The caramel sauce will pool around the custard.

attrs.symptom: The custard has a grainy, curdled texture.
attrs.cause: The milk was too hot when added to the eggs.
attrs.fix: Temper the eggs: add the warm milk very slowly at first, whisking constantly. The milk should be warm, not hot.

attrs.symptom: The custard has bubbles on the surface.
attrs.cause: The custard mixture was whisked too vigorously.
attrs.fix: Whisk gently and strain the custard before pouring. Pop any surface bubbles with a kitchen torch or the tip of a knife.

attrs.symptom: The caramel at the bottom has crystallised and does not flow.
attrs.cause: The caramel was cooked with a lid or stirred too early.
attrs.fix: Cook caramel without stirring and without a lid. Once it turns amber, remove from heat immediately to prevent it going grainy.

content.text: Where this dish lives
Bánh flan was introduced to Vietnam during the French colonial period and has been fully adopted into Vietnamese food culture.
It is sold at bakeries, cafés, and street food stalls throughout the country.
Vietnamese cooks adapted the French crème caramel by using condensed milk, which is widely available.
In Hanoi, it is often served with a drizzle of strong Vietnamese coffee on top.
It is one of the most popular Western-style desserts in Vietnam.
